14.t: Working with data: speed of replication
q: E. coli has one origin. Calculate the time to copy its genome.
Each fork copies 2.3 million bases: 2 300 000 / 1000 = 2300 s = about 38 minutes.
Calculate how long chromosome 1 would take with only one origin.
125 million / 50 = 2 500 000 s = about 29 days.
Chromosome 1 is copied in about 8 hours. Calculate the minimum number of origins it needs.
2 500 000 / 28 800 s = about 90 origins (more in reality, because not all forks run all the time).
Suggest why human replication forks move more slowly than bacterial ones.
Human DNA is wrapped around histones in chromatin, which must be unpacked and repacked as the fork passes.
E. coli can divide every 20 minutes, although copying its genome takes 38 minutes. Suggest how.
It starts new rounds of replication at the origin before the previous round has finished, so a daughter cell inherits DNA that is already being copied.

18.t: Working with data: proofreading and errors
q: Calculate how many times proofreading improves accuracy.
10 million / 100 000 = 100 times.
Estimate the number of errors per human cell division after all checks.
6.4 billion / 10 billion = about 0.6: roughly one new error every one or two divisions.
Estimate the number of errors per division if mismatch repair failed.
6.4 billion / 10 million = about 640.
People who inherit faulty mismatch-repair genes have a much higher risk of cancer. Explain, using your answer to question 3.
Hundreds of times more mutations arise at each division, so it is much more likely that several mutations hit oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes in one cell, letting it divide uncontrollably.
Suggest why a very low, but not zero, error rate is useful for a species.
Rare mutations provide new variation, which natural selection can act on, without harming most individuals.
